title: The Price of Being Seen
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 23 of 40
content:
The newspaper photograph caught Greg in the middle of laughing and me in the middle of looking at him.

It should have been sweet. Instead the caption described me as the person who had finally settled Beach City's most eligible wandering musician, which was a remarkable number of assumptions to pack into fourteen words.

"Most eligible?" Greg said. "I wish somebody had told me."

"That's the part you're worried about?"

"No. That's the part I can joke about without sweating through my shirt."

We stood beside the laundromat's humming washers, reading the little local paper above a rack of detergent. The article was about a neighborhood music night. We'd helped set up microphones and stayed late to stack chairs. Somehow the reporter had decided the important story was my relationship status.

A customer behind us wanted to know whether the next concert would be free. Greg answered her politely and promised to check the community schedule. Then we took the paper to the editor's office two doors down.

She looked exhausted. Ink marked the side of her thumb; a stack of late notices had eaten half her desk.

"I'm glad you liked the picture," she began.

"We didn't come about the picture," I said.

Her smile faltered. "The caption?"

"It says I settled him. I didn't. We chose to spend time together. And there are other people in my life who didn't agree to become part of this story."

The editor's eyes went to Greg.

He raised both hands. "I think Jasper explained it pretty well."

She tapped her pen. "People are interested. Greg's been around forever. It's a local feel-good piece."

"Then let it feel good without claiming we signed an ownership deed," I said.

I heard how sharp I sounded and took a breath. "I'm ethically non-monogamous. I prefer polyamory. Greg knows, and we make our agreements privately. I don't want a headline that pretends he rescued me from every other relationship, or that I'm his reward for being lovable."

Greg looked at the floor and smiled at his shoes.

The editor read the caption again.

"You're right," she said. "I was trying to make a story out of a shortcut."

Greg cleared his throat. "Could you maybe mention the two teenagers who kept the sound board from falling over? They did the actual heroics."

"Not without asking them and their parents," the editor said.

"Good point."

We settled on a correction that named the music night, the performers who had agreed to be credited, and the money raised for instrument repairs. The next issue could carry the correct information. Online or not, the printed copies already out in town weren't going to vanish.

Outside, Greg leaned against the van.

"You okay?" he asked.

"Embarrassed. Annoyed. Weirdly hungry."

"That's a whole album."

"I'd buy it."

He nudged my shoulder with his. "You know, I liked how you said we chose each other."

"It was true."

"I got scared you were going to be mad at me for not stepping in sooner."

"You let me speak for myself. That wasn't abandoning me."

"Good. Because I was also busy thinking of twelve terrible jokes."

"Only twelve?"

"I've got standards."

We got sandwiches from the boardwalk and carried them to the van. Someone had taped a flyer to its window asking Greg to perform at a fundraiser he hadn't heard about. He read it, sighed, and wrote down the contact number. Being liked in a small town meant people assumed you could always say yes.

"You can decline," I said.

"Yeah. I know. I'm trying to remember that."

A gull stole a corner of my sandwich. Greg laughed so hard he nearly lost his drink. I chased the bird a grand total of three steps before realizing the humiliation was complete.

Later, at the car wash office, we drafted a response to the fundraising committee and made a list of gigs he actually wanted to play. We kept separate calendars. He asked which dates affected us; I told him the ones that did. Neither of us needed a report on every other person I saw.

The correction came out the following week. It was small, under the community notices. It gave credit to the musicians and volunteers. It didn't put me on display.

Greg read it twice.

"They spelled my name right," he said. "That's new."

He reached for my hand. I let him take it.

"Can I kiss you?" he asked.

"Yes."

We kissed beside the van where anyone might have seen, and then I drew back laughing at his hair getting caught in the open window.

"You all right?" I asked.

"Romantically compromised," he said.

I shut the window. We kept the rest of the evening for ourselves, not because there was anything shameful to hide, but because some things were ours to choose.
